newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court refuses to delay Clinton lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court refuses to delay Clinton lawsuit.

text.p: A unanimous Supreme Court ruled on Tuesday that Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against President Bill Clinton can go forward, rejecting his argument that it should wait until he leaves office.

The nation's highest court dealt Clinton a major setback by rejecting his claim that a president, while in the White House, enjoys temporary immunity from civil lawsuits seeking damages for events that occurred before he took office.
The nine justices, including two appointed by Clinton, held that the U.S. Constitution does not require that the politically embarrassing lawsuit be placed on hold until he leaves office in 2001.

The ruling involved only the issue of when the case goes forward, not the merits of Jones' allegations that Clinton made unwanted advances in 1991 in a Little Rock hotel room when he was governor of Arkansas and she was a state employee.

She claimed Clinton had her summoned during a government conference and when they were alone exposed himself to her and asked her to perform oral sex. Jones, who seeks $700,000 in damages, wanted the lawsuit to proceed without delay.
Lawyers for Jones said they would hold a news conference in Washington at 2:30 p.m. (1830 GMT) to discuss the Supreme Court ruling. Jones herself would not be attending, they said.

Clinton has denied the allegations. "I have nothing to say at the moment. We're going to have to talk to counsel," White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn told reporters in Paris when asked about the court's ruling.

Clinton's attorney, Robert Bennett, had argued that suits against an incumbent president must be delayed "in all but the most exceptional cases" because they would be "burdensome and disruptive," distracting from the duties of the job. He said no U.S. president had ever been required to give evidence in a civil proceeding, much less appear as a defendant in court.

Bennett and Clinton sought not only to postpone a trial in the case but also to delay questioning of Clinton or any witnesses until he leaves office on Jan. 20, 2001, when his successor will be sworn in. But Justice John Paul Stevens, writing for the court in a landmark 28-page opinion, flatly rejected all of those arguments.

He said allowing the case to go forward would not place "unaccpetable burdens" on the president hampering the performance of official duties. Stevens also said federal courts have the power to decide the legality of the president's unofficial conduct.

"The federal district court has jurisdiction to decide this case. Like every other citizen who properly invokes that jurisdiction, (Jones) has a right to an orderly disposition of her claims," he wrote.
He rejected Clinton's claims that allowing the case to proceed would generate a large volume of politically motivated harassing and frivolous lawsuits against the president.

The next step will be for the case to go back to a federal judge in Arkansas, where it was filed in 1994. The judge may decide whether to force Clinton to submit to pre-trial questioning and then a trial.

The high court's ruling could place pressure on Clinton to settle the controversy. There have been unsuccessful efforts to settle the lawsuit, once before it was filed and again a year ago before the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case.
